newsitem.title: USA: Kodak shrs get no bounce, EPS views trimmed.
newsitem.headline: Kodak shrs get no bounce, EPS views trimmed.

text.p: Eastman Kodak Co shares fell further Monday after going into a tailspin Friday on news that lower prices and a strong dollar had contributed to a slower start for the company in 1997 versus last year.

In late-morning New York Stock Exchange trade, the photography giant's shares were off 7/8 to 77-5/8, trading just above the session low 77-1/4 in unusually brisk activity that put Kodak atop the NYSE most-active list.
With less than half the trading session gone, volume of about 2.3 milion shares was almost twice Kodak's daily average.

Kodak Chief Financial Officer Harry Kavetas said Friday, "Although 1997 has started more slowly than we expected, there is nothing in these first months which would cause us to change our fundamental operating plans and objectives."
The stock tumbled 9-1/4 to 79 Friday. With today's further decline, the share price is at its lowest point since late October 1996.
Further weighing on the stock this morning was Salomon Bros's cutting the stock to hold from buy and reducing 1997 and 1998 per-share earnings estimates.
In a research note, Salomon analyst Jonathan Rosenzweig said he had cut his 1997 estimate to $4.80 per share from $5.05, and his 1998 estimate to $5.60 from $5.90.

"It is important to emphasize that our decision to cut the (rating) code does not merely reflect the company's poor performance during the first two months of the year. Rather, several issues have altered our fundamental thesis," the analyst wrote.
He said Salomon's buy rating had been based on three factors: success of the new Advanced Photo System film format, international expansion, and strong single-use camera sales.

"Lackluster performance for the APS could necessitate additional investment by Kodak," Rosenzweig said, adding that a Salomon survey and market sources indicate sales of APS cameras, film and processing have been below expectations.

Also, "Emerging market sales could be hindered by difficulties in China for several quarters," he said, and "single-use camera sales remain strong, but the growth rate has slowed and competition is intense."
